name: Ambassador
intent: Put a helper beside a client that represents a remote service and handles its retries, timeouts and failures for it.
scenario: Five apps call a partner's exchange-rate API, which fails now and then. Each app has its own idea of when to retry and when to give up.
problem: Each app calls the partner directly. One retries at once and hammers the partner, one never retries, and when the partner is down every app keeps trying and waits on every call.
solution: An Ambassador runs next to each client, on the same host, and speaks for the remote service. The app asks it for a rate as if it were the partner. The ambassador sets timeouts, retries with limits and stops calling a partner that is clearly down (a circuit breaker). It reports a clear failure to the app. The policy is written once and applied to every client.
pain: Each app has its own retry rules, and some are harmful
A partner outage makes every call slow before it fails
Retries from many apps add load to a service that is already struggling
Changing the policy means changing every app
benefits: One retry and timeout policy for every client
A down partner is detected and spared extra traffic
Apps see a quick, clear answer: a value, or a failure
The policy is tuned or replaced without touching the apps
whenToUse: Several clients, possibly in different languages, call the same unreliable remote service
You want consistent timeouts, retries and circuit breaking in one place
The remote service cannot be changed, such as a partner or a legacy system
whenNotToUse: One client in one language: a client library with the same policy is simpler
A remote call that must never be repeated unless it is idempotent, and the ambassador cannot tell
When you would have to run an extra process per client with no one to operate it
pitfalls: Retrying calls that are not idempotent can repeat a payment or an email
Retries without backoff and a limit turn a small partner problem into an outage
The ambassador becomes one more thing that can fail, and apps must treat its failure clearly
A shared ambassador serving many hosts is a central proxy, and loses the benefit of sharing fate with its client

roles.label: Client app
roles.description: Needs data from the remote service. It talks only to the ambassador.

roles.label: Ambassador
roles.description: Runs beside the client. Adds timeouts, retries and a circuit breaker to calls it makes on the client's behalf.

roles.label: Remote service
roles.description: The unreliable service, such as a partner API.

quiz.question: Five apps call a partner API. One retries instantly in a loop, one never retries, and one waits 60 seconds on every failure. What is the best way to get consistent, safe behaviour?
options: Send an email to each team that explains the rules for timeouts and retries
Ask the partner to make its API more reliable, so that no app needs to retry
Run an ambassador beside each app, applying one policy with backoff and timeouts
Remove all retries from the apps, so that a failure is always shown to the user
quiz.explanation: The ambassador puts a single policy beside every client, whatever language it uses. An email leaves five implementations, the partner may not change, and removing retries throws away recoveries that would have worked.

quiz.question: The partner is down for ten minutes. Each of 100 clients tries every request three times, so the partner receives three times the traffic it normally gets and cannot recover. What should the ambassador add?
options: A circuit breaker that stops calls after repeated failures and probes occasionally
A longer timeout on every call, so that clients wait for the partner to come back
More retries per request, so that at least one of them reaches the partner
A cache that returns the last answer for ever, even after the data is out of date
quiz.explanation: Once the partner is clearly down, more calls only slow its recovery. A circuit breaker opens, fails fast, and tries a probe now and then. Longer timeouts and extra retries add load, and an unlimited stale cache serves wrong data.

quiz.question: A team deploys one shared ambassador for all 50 hosts, in a central cluster. Soon one overloaded app slows the ambassador for all of them. What was the mistake?
options: The shared ambassador should have had a larger cache so that it called the partner less
The shared ambassador should have used a faster programming language than the apps use
The apps should have called the partner directly whenever the ambassador is slow
An ambassador belongs beside its client, so that a problem stays with one client and not all
quiz.explanation: Running the ambassador on the client's host keeps failures and load local and avoids a central bottleneck. A larger cache, a faster language or falling back to direct calls do not remove the shared dependency.
